                            REPLY BRIEF


       COMES NOW, Cherokee Creek Partners, Bonnie Helene McAnelly, Individually and as

Trustee of the 2025 Homestead Trust and The Bonnie Helene McAnelly 2023 Trust, Bernareggio

Family Partners, Ltd., Robert Bowling, and Wendell and Shirley Fleming (“Cherokee Creek

Aligned Intervenors”) and files their Reply Brief (the “Reply Brief”) to the Application of Oncor

and LCRA TSC (“Joint Applicants,” or “Oncor” and “LCRA TSC,” respectively) for the above to

amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN” or “Application”). Cherokee

Creek Aligned Intervenors pray that the Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) issue a Proposal for

Decision (“PFD”) recommending the Texas Public Utility Commission (“PUC”) approve

Cherokee Creek Route G (“Route CCG”).
       I.       INTRODUCTION

               These cases are challenging. They are personal for the landowners and the
               affected communities. It is important that the Commission get these cases right.
               Part of getting it right means following the law and evaluating all of the
               statutory and rule factors in a reasoned way. While it is tempting to reduce the
               analysis to a numerical exercise that gives a feeling of objectivity, doing so
               would not be consistent with the public service role of the Commission. 1
                                                    Former PUC Chairman Barry Smitherman


           The initial briefs supporting Routes 894 and 487 share a common and fundamental flaw:

they treat a handful of quantitative metrics—cost, habitable structure counts, and route length—as

though those figures were sufficient to end the inquiry. They are not. PURA § 37.056(c) and 16

TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require a holistic balancing of all statutory and rule factors, and no single

factor or cluster of factors is dispositive. As the court recognized in Dunn v. Public Utility

Commission, the plain language of the Commission’s rules grants the PUC authority to evaluate

and balance a variety of routing considerations, with none controlling the outcome. 2

           The parties supporting Routes 894 and 487 elevate these quantitative figures,

disproportionately weighing their significance. Minor differences in cost or habitable structure

counts, particularly where those differences fall within the range of cost-estimate uncertainty

acknowledged by the Joint Applicants, do not resolve the question before the Commission. The

question is not which route scores best on the most metrics. It is which route, on a careful and

reasoned balancing of all required criteria, least harms the community and the landowners affected

while still complying with the statute and applicable rules.

             When the full statutory framework is applied to the record here, Route CCG emerges as

the route that best balances all applicable criteria, particularly in comparison to Route 894 and 487.

Route 894’s advantages on habitable structure count and cost fall only within a modest difference

and engineering contingency. Its paralleling advantage rests overwhelmingly on property

boundaries, not real infrastructure. And it imposes avoidable, lasting harm on 2 irreplaceable state

parks. Route 487 abuts Colorado Bend State Park and performs poorly under the park and aesthetic

impact criteria. Route CCG avoids those harms, performs better across a full range of

environmental integrity criteria, and satisfies all statutory routing factors.

      II.      ROUTE CCG REMAINS THE MOST BALANCED ROUTE IN THE RECORD

            Route CCG was developed specifically to improve upon Routes 894 and 487. Reinecke

reviewed the full route universe of 123 alternatives and designed Route CCG to incorporate the

favorable portions of existing routes while departing from them only where meaningful

improvements could be achieved. 3 The differences between Route CCG and Route 894 are

intentional and consequential—each departure corresponds to a documented improvement in

preserving parks, crossing rivers, or protecting environmental integrity.

            Route CCG outperforms competing routes on paralleling by consolidating disturbance

within existing corridors and paralleling more miles of existing transmission lines, public roads,

and property boundaries than Route 894. 4 Route CCG avoids the Ecologically Significant Stream

Segments (“ESSS”) portion the Colorado River and Rocky Creek, avoids USFWS Karst Zone 1

entirely, avoids the Edwards Aquifer, avoids USFWS-designated critical habitat for the Texas

proceeding achieves the same breadth of environmental protections, landowner considerations,

    III.      ROUTE CCG’S HABITABLE STRUCTURE COUNTY AND COST DO NOT
              OUTWEIGH ROUTE CCG’S SUPERIOR PERFORMANCE ACROSS
              MULTIPLE ROUTING CRITERIA

              a. The Habitable Structure Gap Falls Within One Standard Deviation and Does
                 Not Meaningfully Shift the Outcome.

criterion across the full route universe is approximately 27 structures. 8 A 20-structure gap falls

within one standard deviation. Routes within one standard deviation of each other are, at the very

least, statistically comparable for this specific criterion in this specific case. 9

            b. Route CCG Better Preserves Environmental Integrity Across the Entire Study
               Area.

                   i.    Superior River Crossings at Both the Colorado and San Saba Rivers

        Route CCG optimizes alignment at both major river crossings in the study area. At the

Colorado River, Route CCG uses Links J31-J32, crossing alongside an existing pipeline corridor,

a location that is farther from Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park and that

produces the lowest foreground visual zone exposure of any evaluated alignment by TPWD. 27 At

the San Saba River, Route CCG uses Link L4, crossing alongside an existing American Electric

affected area. 28 This is precisely what TPWD recommended and what the paralleling criteria are

designed to reward. Chairman Smitherman’s 2010 memorandum in Docket No. 37448 established

this Commission’s historical concern about new crossings of the Colorado River in this vicinity

and the importance of using existing corridor infrastructure. 29 Links J22 and J26—used by Route

894—replicate the same problematic Colorado River crossing the Commission previously

rejected. Route CCG’s Links J31-J32 answer that concern directly by using a pre-existing pipeline

                     ii.    Ecologically Significant Stream Segment and Consolidated Disturbance

         The raw stream crossing counts reported in EA Table 7-2 are an inadequate measure of

environmental impact and cannot serve as the basis for a meaningful environmental integrity

determination under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D).

         The Applicants’ witness, Mr. Marusak, conceded under cross-examination that crossing a

major river and crossing a small creek are counted identically in those tabulated numbers. 30 Ms.

Cooley further acknowledged that a proper crossing evaluation requires consideration of the angle

of crossing, surrounding topography, constructability, river adjacency, the presence of USFWS-

designated critical habitat, and whether a crossing falls within an ESSS.31 Cooley also confirmed

that for larger perennial streams and rivers, the Applicants can construct from opposite banks to

avoid any placement of fill in the regulated water body, and that with typical structure spans of

1,400 to 1,500 feet, the Applicants would be able to span a majority of crossings. 32 That the

Applicants possess the engineering capability to treat crossings differently depending on their

sensitivity further underscores that a flat crossing count is meaningless as an environmental metric.

As Reinecke summarized, a minor ephemeral drainage simply does not present the same ecological

and hydrological impacts as a major river crossing with a forested riparian corridor. 33 Because

Table 7-2 treats every crossing as equivalent regardless of ecological significance, reliance on it

alone produces a legally and factually deficient routing analysis.

                 iii.    Golden-cheeked Warbler

     V.      THE PRINCIPAL CRITICISMS OF ROUTE CCG FAIL

             a. Route 894’s Paralleling Advantage is Illusory—it Rests Overwhelmingly on
                Property Boundaries, Not Compatible Infrastructure.

             b. Route CCG’s Additional Length Reflects Deliberate, Justified Routing

              d. The Single-Point-Failure/Resiliency Argument is Speculative, Unquantified,

a hypothetical flood event severe enough to simultaneously take down both the existing 138-kV

line and a new 765-kV structure. Commissioner McAdams has not performed engineering analysis

to determine whether a properly designed 765-kV structure would fail in a flood. 61 He is not an

engineer and has not designed 765-kV structures or foundations. 62 He is not even saying

Route CCG’s demonstrated routing advantages.
